courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Music, Culture and Outreach
courses.description:
It is of crucial significance for cultural practitioners and managers to develop a solid foundation and capability in understanding the nature of music from various perspectives, as well as possessing the competency in appreciating the aesthetic and artistic value of musical works for the sake of advocating, marketing, coordinating and managing various programmes, events and outreach in music. Through exploring a wide range of music literature from different historical periods in music, the course focuses on three main perspectives:

The first perspective focuses on listening and examining the major masterpieces in the history of music from Middle Ages to Modern, in which musical elements and characteristics of major forms and genres will be introduced and analysed. The second perspective is identified by the relationship of music to culture, in which the influence that cultural, social, political and religious events have exerted on music will be discussed. The third perspective focuses on experiencing and examining the approaches of music education in advocating music in the society. Through experiential learning, students will be able to develop basic knowledge and skills for applying the current theories and approaches in music education (e.g. play-based approach, Orff Schulwerk, Dalcroze, Kodaly) to outreach and education in the society.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part I: Basics in Music Appreciation

1. What is “Music Appreciation”?

This session gives an introduction to how to be an ‘educated’ listener’. Major elements and focus of listening in appreciating the aesthetic and artistic value of music will be introduced.

2. Roles of Music in the Society

This session discusses the roles of music in the society and various impacts of music will be discussed. Also, this section investigates how cultural, social, political and religious events have influenced the development of music.

3. Understanding Orchestration

This session uses musical excerpts and examples to illustrate the characteristics and timbre/tone colour of a wide range of orchestral instruments, as well as various concepts on orchestration.

4. Field Trip

Field trip to a music institution (e.g. orchestra) will be arranged for students to gain a deeper understanding on the various aspects of performance as well as management of music institutions.

Part II: A Journey to Appreciating Music

5. Music in Middle Ages (500-1400) and Renaissance (1450-1600)

This session introduces the main characteristics of Middle Ages and Renaissance music. Major genres and musical styles of the Middle Ages will be discussed, e.g. Gregorian Chant, Mass, Estampe, Rondeau. Featured genres in the Renaissance will also be discussed, e.g. Motet, Mass, Madrigal, Lute Song, Polychoral Motet. Through exploring the musical works of Middle Ages and Renaissance, the interrelationship among music, culture and society will be discussed.

6. Music in the Baroque Period (1600-1750)

This session studies the main characteristics and musical style of Baroque music. Major forms and genres of Baroque music will be introduced and analysed, e.g. Opera, Solo Concerto, Prelude and Fugue, Cantata, Oratorio, Suite. Through exploring the musical works of Baroque period, the interrelationship among music, culture and society will be discussed.

7. Music in the Classical Period (1750-1820)

This session studies the main characteristics and musical style of Classical Period. Major forms and genres of Baroque music will be introduced and analysed, e.g. sonata form, theme and variation, rondo, classical symphony, classical concerto.

8. Music in the Romantic Period (1820-1900)

This session studies the main characteristics of Romantic period. Romantic art songs, operas, programme music, and instrumental works will be introduced and analysed. Through exploring the musical works of Classical period, the interrelationship among music, culture and society will be discussed.

9. Modern Music (1900-Present)/Music of Non-Western Cultures

This session studies the main characteristics of modern music. For example, expressionism, impressionism, 20th century nationalism, and Jazz music will be introduced and analysed. This session also examines the characteristics, musical styles, genres, instrumentation of music from non-western culture, e.g. music in sub-Saharan Africa, classical music of India, Koto music of Japan. Through exploring music of non-western cultures and the musical works of modern period , the interrelationship among music, culture and society will be discussed.

Part III: Bringing the Joy of Appreciating Music through Education

10. Current Theories and Practices in Music Education

This session focuses on discussing the current theories, thoughts, and approaches in music education, e.g. Developmentally Appropriate Practice (DAP), Play-Based Approach, Orff Schulwerk, and Dalcroze Approach. The application of these approaches and theories to music appreciation activities in outreach programmes will be discussed.

11. Workshop in Music Pedagogies (I)

Through experiential learning and firsthand experience, this session introduces the skills and techniques in movement and choreography for conducting outreach and education in music. Musical excerpts discussed in Part II will be used as examples for illustration.

12. Workshop in Music Pedagogies (II)

Through experiential learning and firsthand experience, this session introduces the skills and techniques in singing and chanting, and the application of percussion instruments for conducting outreach and education in music. Musical excerpts discussed in Part II will be used as examples for illustration.

13. Presentation and Conclusion

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Visual Arts Management
courses.description: This course leads students to study various modes and philosophies of visual arts management undertaken in different venues. Aesthetics and art criticisms are critical in directing art interpretation and presentation. Contemporary management of visual arts responds predominantly to the worldwide discussions on modernism as well as various post-modernist writings. In addition, it has to operate in accordance with the prescribed state policy. For this bilateral concern of art management, the course comprises two sections. The first section leads students to study the writings on aesthetics by critics from Plato to Foucault, whose arguments are still valid in inspiring many art exhibitions. The second section discusses the practical concerns and techniques in maximizing the social and economic impacts of art exhibitions and relevant events. Both sections discuss case studies taken from different parts of the world.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe different categories of visual arts in professional language; to define and explain the key terms in visual art literature; to appreciate and analyze art exhibitions with reference to intellectual debates on aesthetics; to describe and explain the art policies implemented in East Asia and the West; and to develop independent thinking on the operation and promotion of art organizations.
courses.course_syllabus:
Section I: Aesthetics and art criticisms

1. Introduction: Shifting perspectives on visual art management in the 20th century
Visual art management was a new discipline born in late 19th century when museums appeared in Europe. This session reviews the early practices in museum curatorship and its transformations under the impact of modernism. It explains how the focus in managing visual art shifted from scholarly field to public arena in the 21st century.

2. ‘Is it good art?’: From Plato, Hume to Danto on aesthetics
‘What is beauty?’ has been the most discussed topic in Western art history since the times of Plato. This session discusses the canonical writings by Plato and his followers and critics during the times of Renaissance. The discussion links to their contributions to the post-modern theories that still weigh importantly today.

3. Visuality and Perception
The intention of artists and the perception of arts of the beholders are core issues in Western aesthetics. This section discusses the most well-read writings by Ernest Gombrich and John Berger, who respond to the question as to whether arts comprise social values.

4. ‘Does Fine Arts still stand today?’: From fine arts to commercial arts
Visual arts comprise a wide range of categories today that include both traditional oil paintings and sculpture, as well as contemporary art forms that includes installation, and industrial designs. This section discusses the shifting definitions of arts and the incorporation of commercial arts in exhibitions.

5. Cross-cultural aesthetics
Are Western art theories applicable to the Asian contexts? Correlation exists between civilization and visual culture. This session discusses the Chinese visual art system and explains its difference from that in the West.

Section II: Concerns and Practices

6. Writing and arts
This lecture analyzes different texts about visual arts taken from museum exhibition catalogues, auction house catalogues, newspaper reviews, as well as commercial gallery publications. This leads students to reflect on the different presentations of arts for education and commercial purposes.

7. Arts and state
This lectures discusses the various policies implemented in the US, UK, and China that enables or hinders the developments of art organizations and individual artists.

8. Business and Arts
Artists and art organizations s management relies heavily on the patronage of business firm. This session discuss the mutual relationship between arts and business, as well as their shifting roles in recent decades.

9. Audience and arts
This lecture extends the discussion of the last, and focuses on the concerns and strategies of art and cultural promoters in non-profit, educational sectors. This introduces the issue of branding implemented in many world renowned institutes and evaluates their success.

10. Managers and arts
This lecture discusses human resources management in the art industry. Examples of excellent directorship taken from the UK and US will be studied to shed light on the significance of professional leadership in the discipline.

11. The Biennial fever
Bienne is world recognized art event to showcase and acknowledge the achievements of young artists. This lecture discusses the organization and social impacts of the bienne festivals held in Europe and Asia.

12. Artist villages
Artist village is developing everywhere in the world. This lectures discusses the examples found in China and Taiwan and leads students to think whether Hong Kong will need an artist cluster for future cultural developments.

13. Art events and festivals
Annual art events and festivals serve as major strategies to generate social and economic support for art today. This lecture discusses the organization and planning of those events and evaluate the examples taken from Europe, US and Asia.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Performing Arts Management
courses.description: This course discusses the missions, administrations, and strategies of performing art organizations. Since the 1950s, performing art managers have realized the significance of efficient management in achieving popularity and sale. This course will go through the general topics as to how the performing art organizations are administered in national and legal terms; how they solicit funding; how they are operated in terms of ticketing and touring; and how they are strategically promoted for both branding and social benefits.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to describe the practical concerns of the performing art organizations in terms of their daily operation; to identify various sources of funding in support of performing arts; to evaluate the administration structure and strategies undertaken in different countries; and describe and explain the different policies implemented in East Asia and the West.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Introduction: Profit-making vs Non-profiting making performing houses
This lecture introduces the basic, binal division between two different types of performing houses. This leads students to reflect on the confliciting aims between the two types, and realize the significance of the overlapping features of the two.

2. Setting up the ‘mission’
Clear directorship is recognizedly important among performing arts management. This lecture analyzes the various mission statements and approach of the performing houses in Europe, US and China. This discusses how a mission statement is being written up and executed.

3. Legal rights and obligations of non-profit making organizations.
This lecture discusses the legal terms of the non-profiting making performing organizations, and provides an in-depth study towards their social obligations in exchange for tax exemption.

4. Commercial productions.
This lecture discusses the concerns and strategies of Broadway productions. Examples of programming and touring techniques of the theatres in the US, France and China will be discussed.

5. Budget planning
Financial management in the performing industry aims to maintain balance between expenses and revenue. This lecture discusses the management of book keeping, payroll taxes, facilities maintenance, and auditing.

6. Fund-raising possibilities for non-profit performing houses
There are many fund-raising opportunities for non-profit organizations. Managers usually have to work closely with the Board of Directors. Tactics in securing interests and long-term partnerships with external and potential donors will be discussed.

7. Sale and ticketing
Following up with the last session, this lecture discusses the marketing management of commercial productions. The role of ticket office and various advertising skills will be compared and discussed.

8. Performing arts and education
This lecture discusses the American tactics in engaging junior and high school students in performing arts. It discusses the experience of the New York City Centre and the Kennedy Centre. This session invites students to reflect on the social impacts of the performing industry through arts education.

9. Human resources
Theatres and Orchestras work closely with large numbers of members from various sorts of backgrounds. Management in labor relations has always been a key to achieve success in the performing industry. This section introduces various labour unions and legal regulations towards employment contracts.

10. Touring production
Touring is a common tactic employed to increase revenue by taking the performing crew overseas. However, touring means many risks that may increase expenses. This lecture discusses the benefits and shortcomings in taking a production on a tour.

11. Facility management
Facilities maintenance assumes a large share of expense on the financial sheet of presenters. This session discusses the contracting tactics in keeping the costs low. In addition, it also discusses event programming that draws attention to the management of facilities.

12. Internship and youth programmes
This lecture discusses the outreach options for performing houses. It will focus on the networking and partnership formed on the basis of short-term internship; and on the audience-engaging programme that develops the audience base of different age range.

13. Presentation
Student presentation of group project.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Animals, Culture and Modern Society
courses.description:
(UGEC3481 is double-coded with CURE3003.)

How do we understand and connect to animal kingdom?
How do human-animal connections shape modern culture and society?
How do cultural studies and humanities expand our scope on animal and nature?

Culture is ordinary, in Raymond William’s saying, but the ordinariness is merely treated as a reflection of human everyday life. Although cultural studies has sustained concern on everyday life with mass production, consumerism, sexism, racism and postmodernism, the discipline always lags behind the concern of nature and animal species. As the issues of animal abuse, environmental protection, factory farming, animal protection policy and law-making, as well as media various portrayals being the hot topics of our (post)modern world, the study of animal with the perspective of cultural studies and other humanity disciplines can explore the possibilities of better human-animal relationship. This course is designed with an empathic concern of other-than-human animals. By exploring different issues of human and animals’ life, this course looks for a harmonious balance of nature and modern culture.

This course focuses on three areas, through which we can explore the different aspects of animal and cultural studies. These areas are:
A. Entering Jurassic Park – Remaking Animals in Leisure (Lecture A1-A4)
B. Attacking Godzilla – Representing Animals in Media (Lecture B1-B4)
C. Finding Nemo – Revitalizing Animals in the City (Lecture C1-C4)

Each area covers a set of animal issue discussion. Area A, apart from theorizing animal with cultural studies, tackles the basic animal issues: pet-nurturing, zoo-building, forest-sustaining and tourism. This is to provide a foundation for understanding animals with a critical reflection of everyday life.

Area B, set with the concern of media, discusses issues of animal representation in cartoon, cinema, literature and journalism. This is to read how animals would be represented and how this affects human understanding and related policy-making. A screening will be run after Lecture Area B. This is to provide an alternative understanding of animal representation in popular media.

Area C further deals with the matters of animal-city relationship in seeing how dogs and cats, cattle and swine, and fishes and dolphins are (mal)treated in the street, the farm and the sea respectively. This is to end the course with a leading thought of perfect balance of nature and modernity; and more queries of human-animal relationship will be raised for contemplation.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Community Making and Public Humanities
courses.description:
This course prepares students to learn from the emerging practices of community making. Through an introduction to the basic concepts, exploration of the origins, development, and implementation, students will understand the emerging intervention methods of humanities in the public domain.

Community making is closely related to sustainable development, involving the application of interdisciplinary theories. Special attention will be given to practical case studies in this course, helping students examine community making practices in the local and neighboring regions, including Japan, Mainland China, and Taiwan. Students will also have the opportunity to personally understand the lived experiences of different communities/groups, and cross-reference them with relevant theories to deepen their understanding.

In this course, students will acquire knowledge on how community making affects community cultural history, construction of collective identity, community participation, cross-sectoral collaboration, and the accumulation of social capital. This course will guide students to initially grasp the roles and collaborative dynamics among the diverse stakeholders in the community, including government departments, social welfare organizations, civic groups, and community organizations, as well as advisory frameworks.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Equips with a multifaceted understanding of community development and civic engagement from a public humanities perspective.
2. Contextualize community making practices within broader sociocultural, historical, and policy landscapes.
3. Critically analyze the complex ecologies of community making.
4. Distinguish community making from traditional approaches, and apply asset-based, participatory frameworks to foster sustainable, community-driven development.
5. Leverage theoretical perspectives to explain the relational dynamics and meaning-making processes shaping community life.
6. Conduct comparative analyses of community making practices across East Asian regions, extrapolating transferable insights for localized application.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1: Make a Difference in Your Community: “Community Making”**

* Introducing the origins, development, and implementation of community making in Hong Kong under various contexts, including “place making” and “community making” concepts.

* *Week 2: Current Ecology of Community Making in Hong Kong**

* Introducing the current situation and ecology of community making in Hong Kong. Learn about the impact of government restructuring regional cultural and recreational community making projects in context of the “improving governance at the district level”.

* *Week 3: Intervention of history, culture and art in the community**

* Learn about the differences between community making and community work. Introducing key aspects of "Asset based Community Development", concerned with how to link micro-assets to the macro-environment, to achieve sustainable community-driven development.

* *Week 4: Symbolic Interactionism and Collective Identity**

* Introducing the weaving of community relationship networks through community making, and how shared identities, values, and goals emerge through social interaction and collective action within a community.

* *Tutorial Case Study:**

- Art Invention / Socially engaged Art in the community

- 林喜兒、霍文芔：《屋宇平民誌 ──記大坑西新邨：香港最後的「私營廉租屋」》 （香港：留下書舍，2024）

- Introduces how “community newspaper” has emerged recently, and how it focuses on humanities aspects, becoming a community platform to organize cultural activities.

* *Week 5: Practical Scenarios of Co-creation, Social Innovation**

* Introducing the concept of social innovation, in which breaking through the division of labor between professions and sectors, encouraging multi-stakeholder cross-sectoral collaboration.

* *Tutorial Case Study****:**

- Social Lab / Innovation lab run with government agencies and citizens to design services and policies for a better public life, through community participation, design thinking and co-creative experiments.

- Revitalization project, how business activates community sustainability?

* *Week 6\*: Field Study: “****Community Living Room” (CLR)**

* Knowing the new pilot programme - community living room. Interact with subdivided house families to understand their views on Community Living Room and the communities they belong to.

* *Tutorial Case Study:**

- Introducing Common Living Room (CLR) run by a private enterprise, and how they use local culture and art as media, and respond to the emerging cultural phenomenon among the young generation in the community by planning different art and experiential activities.

- 鄒崇明、黃英琦、梁志遠、龍子維：《重構香港：從庶民空間到社區更新》（香港：印象文字，2016）

- Introducing the Community Art Developmental Project "Tin Library - Tin Shui Wai Story Gallery" of the Jockey Club Tin Shui Wai Integrated Social Service Centre, which make use of community creation to exploit community resources and promotes creative community projects, enhance community participation, renovate public spaces, and allow residents to discover the experience of co-creation, reconstructing different aspects of life experience in the local neighbourhoods.

* *Week 7: Social Connection and Cultural Diversity in East Asia (1)**

* Review valuable experience from Japan and Taiwan, knowing the complexity of different social structures and cultures. Introducing the concept of community imagination and regional revitalization.

* *Tutorial Case Study:**

- Experience of Tokyo non-profit organization, using historic buildings and private spaces in community making.

- Experience of Taiwan Hualien in rural communities making, young people using culture and art as a medium to interact with different ethnic groups and communities in the district.

* *Week 8: Social Connection and Cultural Diversity in East Asia (2)**

* Review valuable experience from Mainland China, knowing how community making is localized and developed. Exploring how the theory and practice of community self-organization is combined with governance theory.

* *Tutorial Case Study:**

- Experience of Shanghai, creating a Xinhua 15-minute life circle where everyone can participate. Introduce how art and culture are used to connect residents within the community.

- Experience of Wuhan, community making experiment in youth rental community. Introducing local community making team's planning of public art and cultural projects such as "Community Micro-Garden" and "Community Shared Living Room" to broaden grassroots youth's imagination of community life and rebuild social capital.

* *Week 9: Reading Week and Midterm Paper Submission**

* The mid-term paper aims to examine students’ preliminary understanding of concepts or theories taught in this course. Students can select topics that inspires you and gives you a new understanding in community making and public humanities for an in-depth discussion. (Number of words: approx.1000 words)

* *Suggested Framework:**

- What kind of community making projects have you been exposed to or participated in your daily life? What role did you play?

- Observe how different networks of people collaborate within the community? (E.g. residents' organizations, political organizations, arts and cultural groups.) What community making projects have been held?

- The impact of community policies on community creation.

- Introduce a community making case that interests you. Why?

* *Week 10:** **Field Study: “****Transitional Housing” (TH)**

* Knowing the new pilot programme - transitional housing. Are there rooms for community making in short-term vacant land and premises?

* *Tutorial Case Study**

- Introducing how the concept of co-living promotes community engagement and Tong Lau culture.

- Introducing the social housing platform, which combines the roles of social workers and real estate agents to find "good owners" for subdivided housing users.

* *Week 11: Conclusion and Consultation Week (Attendance required****）**

* Summarizing the course, students are divided into groups to prepare for group presentations. Introducing research methods, formats, and topic choices that can be used for student group presentations.

* *Week 12 (and 13): Group Presentation**

* The aim of this presentation is to examine whether students have initially grasped relevant concepts of community making and the importance of promoting collaboration among diverse stakeholders in the community for humanistic care through practice. Students can select topic from the provided list or propose their own for the presentation:

1. Design their own community making projects in historical, cultural or artistic ways aiming to
connect different groups in the community, such as community renewal, community tours, etc.
2. Design collaborative projects to meet the needs of specific groups, such as subdivided housing
residents, elders living alone, aboriginal residents, etc.
3. Start with realistic-themed movies or literary works to discuss the policies and stakeholders
involved in community issues, try to set up community collaboration projects for related issues.

* *Individual final paper****（****Approx. 1500 words****）**

* Each student is required to writes a reflection paper based on the content of the group presentation, which should include the following:

* Brief introduction to the concept of public humanities and its focus on community engagement and social impact.
* Reflections on both peers and personal experiences participating in the community making initiatives.
* Descriptions of interactions with community members and insights learned.
* Discuss how public humanities can promote greater inclusion, representation, and empowerment within the community, using examples from own experiences.
* Connections between academic coursework and practical application of humanities-based knowledge in the community setting.
* Concluding thoughts on the transformative potential of public humanities to address community needs and promote social changes.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Writing Workshop: Cultural Criticism, Media Writing, and Transmedia Storytelling
courses.description:
This course explores the art of writing across various formats and media. Designed to enhance students’ critical and creative capabilities, the course is divided into three parts: cultural criticism, media writing, and transmedia storytelling.

The first section focuses on the function, language, and format of cultural criticism. The course introduces the core principles of writing critique on literature, films, popular culture, and visual art. Students are invited to discuss the works both aesthetically and critically.

Another section of the course focuses on the fundamental skills specific to the media forms of print, digital platforms, and social media. Foregrounded with a comprehensive understanding of media infrastructures, students will be able to develop skills in collecting information, generating ideas, organizing the structure of their writing, and effectively presenting their thoughts.

The final section draws on Henry Jenkins’s concept of “convergence.” We will compare the conventions of traditional narratives with the world of transmedia storytelling, including but not limited to the ‘converging’ realms of YouTube, podcasts, and interactive content on social media. Students will learn to develop storytelling skills while making good use of media platforms for content distribution.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* State and recognise the definition of criticism, media writing and transmedia storytelling.
* List and clarify principles and skills to structure their criticism, media writing and transmedia storytelling.
* Apply various strategies to enchant their language and improve their accuracy, clarity and conciseness in writing criticism.
* Create and design media content and transmedia storytelling with critical thinking.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part 1 Criticism

Lesson 1 Writing and Storytelling in the Transmedia Era

Lesson 2 What is Criticism? From Aesthetics to Politics

Lesson 3 Reading, attributing, quoting, and structuring your article

Lesson 4 The language of criticism: accuracy, clarity and conciseness

Lesson 5 Workshop I: Arts & Cultural Criticism

Lesson 6 Discussion and Reflection (Peer-reading and reviewing of selected essays.)

Part 2 Media Writing

Lesson 7 Literacy in Media Writing

Lesson 8 Collecting data and information and the curation of story

Lesson 9 Workshop III: Writing Feature Story

Part 3 Transmedia Storytelling

Lesson 10 What is Transmedia Storytelling? Intertextual Commodities and Transmedia Branding

Lesson 11 Workshop IV: YouTube & Podcast

Lesson 12 Workshop V: Social Media and Interactive Content

Lesson 13 Discussion and Reflection II (Peer-reading and reviewing of selected essays.)

courses.description: This course will examine the contemporary theories and researches in the field of developmental psychology, and consider their relevance to the field of Religious Education. Issues of moral development, faith development and spiritual development will specifically be considered. Attention will also be given to the implications of developmental perspectives for prospective religious educators in understanding themselves, the persons with whom they work, and the structures that best promote whole person development.

Week 1: Course Introduction: The Place of Religious Education in Whole Person Development

Week 2: Religious Development in Children

Week 3: Religious Development Through the Lifespan: Adolescence and Adulthood Week 4: Moral Development Across the Life Span

Week 5: Faith Development Across the Life Span Week 6: Religion and Personality Development Week 7: Religion, Value Formation in the Life Cycle

Week 8: Varieties of Religious Experience and the Development of Spiritual Mind Week 9: Loss: Lifespan Approach

Week 10: Death and Dying

Week 11: Gender Issues in Whole Person Development

Week 12: Religious Education, Whole Person Development and Well Being Week 13: Quiz and Course Conclusion

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Religious Texts in Translation
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the theories and practice of translating religious texts. It allows students to become aware of the issues, difficulties and strategies involved in cross-cultural transfer and translation. The phenomenon of cultural accommodation and/or transgression as well as inter-religious dialogue in the process of translation will be critically examined. Selected texts may include Chinese translations of the Bible, the Koran, the Buddhist scriptures, missionary tracts and religious allegories like The Pilgrim's Progress. The English translations of Chinese religious novels like Wu Cheng'en's The Journey to the West and Cao Xueqin's The Story of the Stone will also be analyzed.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Difficulties and contributions of cross-cultural translation (跨文化翻譯的困難和貢獻)

2. Principles and theories of translation (翻譯的原則和理論)

3. Strategies of translating religious texts (宗教文本翻譯的策略)

4. Chinese translations of the Buddhist scriptures (佛經漢譯)

5. Chinese translations of the Bible (中文聖經翻譯)

6. Chinese translations of religious allegory: The Pilgrim’s Progress (宗教寓言小說的漢譯：《天路歷程》)

7. Chinese translations of 19thC missionary tract: The Peep of Day (十九世紀傳教士書冊的漢譯：《正道啟蒙》)

8. Chinese translation of Catholic devotional literature: Joy Comes with Dawn (當代天主教靈修文學的漢譯：《晨光喜露》)

9. English translations of Honglou meng (The Story of the Stone) (《紅樓夢》的英譯)

courses.description: Chinese novels have long been intertwined with religion. While Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist thoughts permeate classical Chinese novels, a large number of modern Chinese novels are peppered with Christian elements. As a lively epitome of Chinese religious culture, these novels also promoted the spread of religious thoughts among the people. This course aims to investigate the interactive relationship between Chinese novels and religion. Students will be guided to examine the religious contents in novels and the ways in which religious thoughts shape the themes, narratives, characterization and language of the novels. Texts selected for reading include classical and modern novels, such as Strange Tales of Liaozhai, The Story of the Stone and The Journey to the West.

3. 學生能分析中國小說中的宗教內涵和象徵意義。

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: The Religious Policy and Practices in China Today
courses.description: This course studies the religious policy in China, focusing on: 1) the Constitution, legislation and official statements as they relate to the question of religion; and 2) implementation and accommodation for various religious practices during different political periods.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. 掌握新中國成立迄今黨國宗教政策的演變
2. 從政教關係的脈絡下認識不同宗教的發展空間
3. 認識中國宗教自由的現況及限制
courses.course_syllabus:
一．導論：政教關係、宗教政策與宗教自由
二．政教關係與宗教政策的回顧：從帝制時期到建國前的中國共產黨
三．毛澤東時代：全能政治的發展
四．反帝愛國：全能政治與宗教革新運動
五．鄧小平時代與鄧後時期：威權體制與改革開放
六．從人民鴉片到「相適應」：新時期宗教理論的發展
七．新時期宗教工作及政策的發展
八．「上有政策，下有對策」：宗教政策的落實問題
九．「五大宗教」的發展與制約
十．民間信仰、新興宗教與邪教問題
十一．中國宗教政策的前膽與展望
courses.feedback_evaluation: Students are welcome to give comments and feedback on the course through emails in Moodle or personal exchanges with instructor and/or tutors. An end-of-term university wide course evaluation will be conducted in class.

1. Kindopp, Jason & Carol Lee, Hamrin,. God and Caesar in China: Policy Implications of Church-State Tensions. Washington, D. C.: Brookings Institution Press, 2004.

courses.description:
(UGED3430 is double-coded with CURE3375.)

This course mainly investigates the relationship between religion and natural sciences. The course will cover the following aspects:
1) historical investigation of the relationship between religion and natural sciences; 2) comparison between methodology of natural sciences and religious studies; and
3) religious dealings with different issues arising from scientific discoveries and technological advancements; ecology and religion; and the nature of science and religion in the postmodern culture.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Public and Community Art

meetings.location: William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408
William M W Mong Eng Bldg 408

courses.description: Public art is considered as an important cultural asset of metropolitan cities, closely related to city images and development. Community art serves as a tool for community development, based on the understanding that expression, mastery and communication through the arts powerfully encode cultural values, thus bringing deeper meanings of experience, participation and involvement, sense of belonging to the general public and the community. This course aims to advance students’ understanding of public and community arts by embedding them in the theoretical discussions and critiques of cities and public spaces and practical experiences. It also imparts the knowledge and skills about managing public arts and actualizing community art programs, and discusses the way to support their development responding to the needs.
courses.learning_outcomes: In terms of knowledge acquisition, students are expected to understand how public and community arts emerged in the context of urban regeneration and community activist movements. Students are encouraged to critically analyze the meanings and social values of public art spaces. In terms of managerial concepts and skills, students will learn how public and community arts are supported by government policies, material resources, infrastructure and training. Students are expected to understand public art commission and reception, to master basic principles of utilizing public art as an urban design strategy, and to apply varying approaches to facilitating community art development, for example, advancing community art education, utilizing the cultural planning approach to assess community based cultural resources and the place-event approach to creating a sense of community attachment.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part I. Understanding Public and Community Art
1. General Introduction
This section begins with displaying a range of public and community art cases and presents an introduction to the course. Three issues are covered in this introductory lecture. First, this section provides the conceptual discussions of public space, public art, and their art forms to enable students to understand what public art space and public art is. Second, this section explores the role of artists in public art space and community development. Third, a historical picture of public art is unfolded, which traces its origin, displays its developing process, and takes a glimpse into its enshrined social values.

2. Understanding Public Art Spaces
How should we understand public art spaces and the public nature of public art? This section embeds these issues into the understanding of a city; it then conveys the ideas that public spaces are socially produced and that city forms are imbued with ideologies. Public art stems from an urban setting and then grows through the urban regeneration movement, which comprises several issues, such as urban image, urban form and urban planning as well as their connections with public art space as a form of representational space. Furthermore, this section explores the public nature of public art by examining the process, by which artists derive value from individual creativity in the studios and immense it into the public space.
Tutorial: Discuss the alternative history of public art (Lacy, 1995, 25–28).

3. Public Art: The Monument
The monument is an important theoretical perspective to conceptualize public art. This section explains what a “monument” is and investigates its role—whether statue, memorial, or public statue—in upholding a value-laden system of Western society. Issues under examination range from the connection between monument and national identity, the power and representation of public arts, the transformative understanding of public art as a monument, and the contradictions of public art.
Tutorial: Discuss the public nature of public art.

4. Critical Issues of Public Art Spaces
Who comprise the “audience” of public arts? What does “intention” mean and what is the “effectiveness” of public art? This section further discusses the theories on critical issues related to public art. This section begins with the discussions of the relevant terms and proceeds to various critical thoughts that challenge the value of public art and question its public nature. Students are expected to be able to analyze public art spaces and public art critically.
Tutorial: Develop critical thinking about public art spaces and public art.

5. Public Arts and Community Cultural Development: Theoretical Underpinnings of Community Art
This section provides a synopsis of the histories and theoretical issues of community art. The origin of community art is traced to the discourse of William Morris’s call for social reintegration of artists and a revival of art in the 19th century. Theoretical issues include the “popular front” and class consciousness, civil rights and identity politics, as well as cultural democracy and exchange. In addition, this section discusses the definitions of community, the role of community art, and the core purposes of community development.
Tutorial: Discuss the question, “What makes art valuable?”

Part II. Public Art Management
6. Commission and Reception of Public Art
Based on the public nature of art, this section analyzes the process of art making, which comprises the elements of audience, context, and meaning. The process includes the following: acquiring cultural approval, arriving in public sites and places, providing visiting experiences with the audience, and generating meanings. Cases of Seattle and New York are used for this study. With regard to art reception, it analyzes the issues of taste, the education of the audience, as well as the relationship of art to society and popular visual culture. In addition, this section also distinguishes performance culture from monumental public art.
Tutorial: Distinguish public art from community art.

7. Public Art and Urban Design
This section presents an urban design approach to commissioning and making public art. It outlines the principles for creating a city image, which consists of five elements, and discusses their connections to public art. Various forms of public art in association with the urban setting and the mechanism of public art utilization as an urban design strategy are also discussed. Students are guided toward understanding the role of public arts in urban design guidelines. Moreover, we also discussed a set of design principles on the relationship between public art and various urban forms and spatial components, aimed at integrating public art into the urban setting as context and reference is discussed.
Tutorial: Conduct design software training.
Assignment: Find a sample of public art (i.e., sculpture) using design principles to assess its location, site, and designs as well as to evaluate its strengths and weaknesses. Write a paper based on the research and use the design software to illustrate the arguments.

8. Government Policies for Public and Community Art Development
The relation between power and public and community art is a critical issue in public and community art management. This section discusses the governmental structure that funds and commissions public art, the infrastructure that underpins public art, and the governmental policies that support community art. The selection of commissions and projects is discussed, along with the process of seeking public and professional responses. International and the local Hong Kong contexts are examined to explore how government policies affect public and community art. In the local context, the role of the Leisure and Cultural Services Department in promoting public art in Hong Kong is adopted as a case study.
Tutorial: Conduct an in-class test.

9. Public Art in Metropolitan Cities
This section analyzes the role of public art in metropolitan cities, especially in the spheres of public transport, public open spaces, and public health system. A number of cases are presented, including forms of public art in the New York Subway system, London Underground and Mass Transit Railway, and the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Hong Kong. The issue of commissioning public arts is revisited in the public art in metropolitan context.
Tutorial: Discuss urban design and public art in Hong Kong.

Part III. Community Art Management
10. Developmental Needs of the Field
How can community art development be supported? What do communities need? This section specifies the scope of cultural policies and the policy climate that community artists and community cultural development require. Moreover, this section discusses the material support that community cultural organizations and artists need, including funding supports and internal infrastructure and exchange.
Tutorial: Discuss the cultural policies for public art in Hong Kong.

11. From Theory to Practice I: Process to Develop Community Arts
From theory to practice, this section offers students a general orientation, which serves as a road map to the community-based art process. Five conceptual territories to advance community-based art as well as requisite techniques to fulfill tasks are introduced in this section, which include the following: 1) contacting people in the community; 2) conducting research on the culture of the community and the people’s perception of their community; 3) taking actions to make art projects; 4) gaining feedbacks from the community; and 5) incorporating these art forms into community art education programs to pass on skills and sustain the impact. The program also includes strategies for planning and organizing community outreach and engagement programs as well as ways to enhance public awareness.
Tutorial: Discuss the process of applying theories in the creation of community art in order to practice and initiate the group project with the community.

12. From Theory to Practice II: Key Issues in Community Art Development
Based on the holistic picture of the steps to develop community arts, this section focuses on certain key and challenging issues in the process, specifically those on research methods and art making. The section introduces qualitative and quantitative research methods for the project of community art development, and students are expected to learn how to identify survey areas, design survey questionnaires, run group discussions, and map cultural mind-sets and assets. Another key issue is how to make arts and work with artists. An artist will be invited to be the guest speaker to give the lesson.
Tutorial: Develop a group project with the community.

13. Review and discussions
Students will present their on-going group projects on community art development, and the professor then provides comments and feedbacks on their projects. Key points of this course will also be reviewed in this class.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Entrepreneurship in the Creative Industries
courses.description: The concept of “creative industry” was proposed by the Labor Party in the U.K. in 1997. It refers to the activities that are embedded in individuals’ creativities, talents and skills, which have the potential for employment opportunities and economic growth through the exploitation of intellectual properties. Creative industry has become a key area in contemporary cultural policies. This course introduces students to the basic knowledge of managing entrepreneurship, which is a key issue in the creative industries. It comprises three parts. The first part provides a general introduction. The second part discusses the nature of entrepreneurship in creative industries and demonstrates the entrepreneurial process, through which, creative ideas are generated, cultural diffusion is stimulated and innovation processes are carried out. It informs students of the key traits of the creative entrepreneurs and the business opportunities and models for entrepreneurship processes in the creative industries. In the third part, it explores the conducive policy conditions to support and encourage entrepreneurship in creative industries.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, a student will:
i) Have their understanding being deepened about creative industries and entrepreneurship
ii) Value and appreciate entrepreneurial spirits in the creative industries
iii) Develop sets of skills for entrepreneurial practices
iv) Understand the policy conditions for entrepreneurship and acquire consultation skills for the government
courses.course_syllabus:
Part 1: General Introduction

Lecture 1: Creative industries and entrepreneurship: A brief introduction
The first lecture in this course will brief the concept of “creative industry” and introduce the key issues of creative industries (e.g., its developmental path, the main traits and its importance to economic growth). Entrepreneurship is a concept key to creative industry development: the creation of new business ventures and the conditions that define corporate venturing will be discussed.
Readings:
CCPR, 2003, 13-26;
Harley et. al., 2013, 58-61

Lecture 2: Key issues for stakeholders in the creative industries: A global perspective
The development of the creative economy is widely concerned by policymakers, regional and local government and the business community. This section will explore how stakeholders face these issues in creative industries. It will also introduce creative industry development and entrepreneurship in Asia.
Readings:
Ghosh and Malloy, 2011, 12-15;
Hui, 2007, 9-29

Part 2: The Entrepreneurial Process

Lecture 3: Cultural diffusion in creative industries
Entrepreneurs always face the challenge of transforming their good ideas into entrepreneurial practices. This section will exemplify this process using cases in different creative sectors in Hong Kong. It will explore the issue of “cultural diffusion” in the creative economy, a process, in which, creativity is produced and disseminated among the audience. The affecting factors (e.g., identity, creative product, business process and technology) will be looked into.
Readings:
Desai, 2011, 109-130;
Wolf, 1999, 45-61

Lecture 4: Innovation processes
Innovation is not equal entrepreneurship, but it could be critical to successful entrepreneurship. This section discusses the scope of innovation, which transforms technical ideas and knowledge into new products or services or production processes. It uses examples of opera concert and film industry to demonstrate the process of innovation.
Readings:
Vickery, 1997, 177-179;
Davis and Scase, 2000, 1-22;
Hetcher, 2011, 70-80

Lecture 5: Entrepreneurship features of creative entrepreneurs
What are the characteristics of creative entrepreneurs? To be successful in creative entrepreneurship, you need to know yourself first. Creative entrepreneurs display the traits different from managers in traditional industrial sectors; they represent the new knowledge workers with creative minds and risk taking spirits. Creative entrepreneurs need to remove the barriers of artistic, economic and marketing considerations. Cases from music industry and film industry will be used to illustrate the issues.
Readings:
Malloy, 2011, 15-18;
Glick, 2008, 73-80

Lecture 6: Exploring business opportunities and models for entrepreneurship
Creative products are delivered on two levels: artists and creative entrepreneurs on the one level; and the state and state entrepreneurship on the other level. This section explores how artists and entrepreneurs are fused, and examines business models for entrepreneurship in media and design industries.
Readings:
Bruin, 2007, 87-106;
Harris and Wegg-Prosser, 2009, 229-248

Lecture 7: Guest lecture: The experience from the industries
One or two guest speakers will be invited from the creative industries to share with the students their entrepreneurial experiences. Students are urged to ask questions and observe the qualities and characteristics of these creative entrepreneurs.

Part 3: Supporting Entrepreneurship in Creative Industry Sectors

Lecture 8: Investment and funding for creative enterprises
This section explores the mechanisms and barriers to creative industries investment. It will also discuss the role of the public sector and the opportunities for problem solving. Partnership, commitment, specialism and genericism are the components that constitute the landscape of investment. This section illustrates the policy context and elaborates the value chain of creative industries investment. A set of tips are provided at the end.
Readings:
Powell, 2010, 175-184;
Fleming, 2007, 107-126

Lecture 9: The synergies of higher education, enterprise and innovation
Universities link creativity to intellectual property and business opportunities. Knowledge spills over from education and R&D programmes at universities and supports creative entrepreneurship in the surrounding community. This section looks at the developing role of universities in the creative industries. It explores various learning and entrepreneurial models for technological innovation and business engagement at universities.
Readings:
Brooks, 1997, 109-129;
Stefik and Stefik, 2010, 17-26

Lecture 10: Human language technologies in the creative industries
Two main technologies in the creative industries, i.e., information and communication technology (ICT) and human language technologies (HLT), are introduced. The key knowledge regards how these language technologies foster entrepreneurship in creative industries. Their practical implications to the creative industries in Hong Kong will be discussed.
Readings:
UNTAD, 2010;
Mitchell, 2016, 4-15

Lecture 11: Incubating entrepreneurship in creative industry clusters
Apart from funding investment, legal protection, technological support and university education, creative industry parks serve as incubators for entrepreneurship in the creative industries. An umbrella concept to be discussed in this section is the “creative milieu,” which is often exemplified by “creative industry parks.” Their characteristics and the central management of the parks in supporting entrepreneurship will be examined.
Readings:
CCPR, 2003, 75-184;
Mommaas, 2004, 507-532;
Maskell, 2000, 1-6;
Scott, 1997, 73-80

Fieldtrip: Visiting creative policy makers
A fieldtrip will be organized to expose students to the government officials at the Innovation and Technology Bureau. It will help them to understand Hong Kong creative industry policies and the intellectual property law.

Lecture 13: Course summary
In the last section, students will deliver their group presentations for feedback and discussion. An overview of the key knowledge in this course will be provided and practical implications will be discussed.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Curating and Managing Arts Festival
courses.description: With a global growing interest in organizing grand scale arts and cultural activities to attract local and overseas audience, arts festivals have become popular urban cultural events for cultural development and for building the reputation of a city. Curating and managing cultural festival is subsequently an important area of studies in cultural management. Curating and managing arts festival is a complex process that requires creative programming, skillful execution and careful financial control. This course not only studies the mode of operations of various types of cultural festivals, including festivals of performing arts, visual arts, film, literary arts and community festive celebration, but also introduces to students the basic skills and knowledge of curating and managing arts festivals, with references to local and overseas examples.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Cultural Festival: an introduction
This session studies the history, social functions and basic modes of operation of cultural festivals, with examples from Hong Kong and fromvarious parts of the world.

2. Various types of festivals and their distinctive characters
This session introduces various types of arts festival, from festivals focusing on specific media, grand scale multi-disciplinary festivals, to community based religious/celebrative events, with emphasis on studying their own distinctive characteristics and special technical requirements.

3. Planning cultural festival 1:
This session focuses on programme planning and coordination, as well as resource management within the institutional and community context.

4. Planning festival 2:
This session deals with the planning of setting up an operation framework, allocation of manpower, design of the technical support and working out an operational schedule for a major arts festival.

5. Planning festival 3:
Funding is an essential part of organizing cultural festivals. This session studies the various ways to seek public and private fund, and ways to do financial planning and to exercise financial control over the running of projects.

6. Planning festival 4:
In addition to curating and implementing programmes, a successful festival also includes much supporting activities, ranging from marketing to educational events. This session focuses on the studies of these supplementary activities in order to get the best results for an arts event.

7. Presentation and discussion
Students are asked to form groups to work on proposals for an arts festival. Students are to do their representations at class, and engage in discussion after the presentations.

8. Curation and programming
This session studies the curation of festival programmes with references to local cultural strength and needs, the use of available resources, as well as a study of the global trends in arts festival.

9. Execution and crisis management
This session studies the security measure for major cultural events, and preparations required for unexpected incidents and crisis.

10. Case studies
Using the Hong Kong Arts Festival and Hong Kong Film Festival for case studies, this session studies the actual implementation of cultural festivals within the specific social, cultural and financial context of Hong Kong.

11. Evaluation and research
The success of a festival depends heavily on responses from the audience, the press and the public, this session studies the application of marketing strategies and its consequent results, and ways to make meaningful evaluation for future development.

12. Critical issues relating to arts festival
As arts and cultural festivals become increasingly prolific, its social and cultural impacts are not to be underestimated. This session takes on a critical review of the impacts, the pro and con of organizing arts festivals, as well as possible alternatives.

13. Review and discussion
This session reviews the entire course and engages students in an over-all discussion.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Global Cultural Theories
courses.description:
Departing from the dominant canon of critical theory, this course aims to introduce students to a wider, more diverse range of theoretical texts and frameworks by marginalized voices and from peripheral locations.
This course seeks to decolonize theory by multiplying the sites of intellectual and critical inquiry. Instead of treating Benjamin, Adorno, Hall, and Grossberg as representative of the corpus of theory, it engages with prevailing discussions in Postcolonial Studies, Modernity/Coloniality, and Black Studies. It moves beyond the call for ‘de-Westernization’ by looking at theoretical texts and frameworks produced in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The course concludes by exploring work about indigeneity, memory, and environmentalism.
The course is designed for advanced undergraduates with familiarity in critical approaches to literature, cinema, art, and media. Classes will grapple with the following questions: What qualifies as theory? Is theory necessarily abstract? What is the relationship of theory to particularity and difference? How can theory be made more attune to its contexts of production, dissemination, and application? How can film and visual art offer sources for theorizing? How might theoretical frameworks respond more significantly to social, economic, and environmental conditions from the restructuring of the capitalist system, expansion of media networks, dissolution of national borders, and deterioration of the climate crisis?
courses.learning_outcomes:
The objectives are:

1. To become acquainted with theoretical texts and frameworks in Cultural Studies by marginalized voices from different peripheral social and geographic contexts
2. To apply theory to analyze the articulation of race, gender, memory, and nature in literature, cinema, art, and media
3. To formulate, develop, write, and revise an original critical essay using global cultural theories
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1: How to Theorize Culture?

Week 2: Postcolonialism

Week 3: Modernity/Coloniality

Week 4: Gender

Week 5: Race

Week 6: Migration and Mobility

Week 7: Media Philosophy

Week 8: Memory and Trauma

Week 9: Indigeneity

Week 10: Ecology and the Non-Human

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Workshop in Creative Content
courses.description: Through workshops, this course aims to cultivate students' creative thinking and abilities of artistic expression. It leads students to explore various art forms, such as graphics, sound, non-fiction narrative, drama, experimental film, and cross/inter-disciplinary arts, etc. Specific projects are planned and executed around particular themes through primarily teacher-student consultations and discussions supplemented by lectures. It helps students grasp creative skills to express their opinions and emotions effectively using audiovisual elements. This advanced practical course requires students to have completed the foundational course CURE2066 Visual Design Foundation in advance.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

1. Develop the creative and technical skills necessary to express students' opinions.
2. Enhance the ability to appreciate and think critically about various forms of artistic works while developing the critical, analytical, and editing skills necessary to evaluate works in progress, both in the student's own projects and those of their peers.
3. Improve students' communication and teamwork skills.
4. Learn how to showcase works and develop the ability to engage in dialogues with society.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week** 1. Course Introduction + Introduction to Various Art Forms

* *Week** 2. Data Collection and Research

To learn effective data collection methods and brainstorm to spark creative ideas.

* *Week** 3. Experimental Film + Photography Workshop

To learn experimental film production and photography techniques, exploring the diversity of visual expression.

* *Week** 4. Artistic Photography + Lighting Workshop

To study artistic photography and lighting design, blending light and shadow to convey artistic beauty.

* *Week** 5. Sound Art + Sound Recording & Editing Workshop

To explore sound recording and sound editing techniques, learning to use sound elements to express emotions.

* *Week** 6. Non-Fiction Workshop

To learn non-fiction narrative skills, cultivating the ability to express real stories.

* *Week** 7. Proposal Presentation

Prepare proposals in advance, discuss, and formulate specific plans for art projects.

* *Week** 8. Shooting and Consultation 1,

Teacher-student consultations and guidance to help students address challenges encountered during creation.

* *Week** 9. Shooting and Consultation2

Teacher-student consultations and guidance to help students address challenges encountered during creation.

* *Week** 10. First Draft Submission and Discussion

Complete initial artistic works and engage in discussions, preliminary assessments, and feedback in class.

* *Week** 11. Consultation3

Teacher-student consultations and guidance to help students address challenges encountered during creation.

* *Week** 12. Revised Draft Submission and Discussion

Revise and improve works based on feedback.

Engage in discussions and provide further comments.

* *Week** 13. Plan of the showcase Discussion

Discuss the works for presentation, including exhibitions and demonstrations on campus and the public.

* *Week** 15. Submission of Final Work

Complete the final version of the artistic work, preparing for the formal exhibition.

courses.description: Process of cultural production and cultural practices at various levels are essential to the training of cultural sensitivity and analysis in cultural studies. This course aims to provide students with on-site experience of cultural production and practices for their reflection and integration of cultural theories and concepts they learnt in regular classes. Students will be introduced to a range of cultural institutions and culture-related non-governmental organizations for a placement of eight weeks between May to July during summer. courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Integrated Studies in Cultural Management
courses.description: This course is continuation of CUMT1001, Introduction to Cultural Management, and looks at cultural management from the macro perspective. Successful culture managers work to maintain healthy balance between culture and its relevant fields of interests, which sometimes could turn harmful or beneficial to the growth and development of the corresponding cultural area. The first session discusses the mutual dependence between culture and various areas, which include laws, economy, community, national interests, and art practitioners. In practice, cultural managers usually have to conform to the values and ethnics of the corresponding countries. For that reason, the second session will look at the approach taken in a few remarkable examples, which Taiwan, China, Singapore, South Korea, U.K., and the U.S.
courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to explain different national and social concerns for preserving culture; to identify the legal and ethnic issues relevant to cultural productions; to identify marketing strategies in cultural promotion; to evaluate the measures for maximizing the input of art practitioners; and to describe the various successful cultural schemes implemented in overseas countries.
courses.course_syllabus:
Section I: Culture in Context

1. Culture & States
The growth of cultural industries is strongly related to political environment and state policy. This lecture discusses the tension and mutual expectations between cultural workers and politicians. It will use the experience of the European Union and the US as examples.

2. Culture & Laws
Over the last few decades, there were a number of remarkable disputes over international art transactions and copy rights. Given the growing size of the art market, knowledge about the previous cases is essential. This lecture takes the examples taken from the US for discussions.

3. Culture & UNESCO
UNESCO is arguably a rising new power in forming a standard for evaluating cultural heritage of different nations. This lecture discusses the roles of UNESCO and its work in different cultural disciplines. National disputes over ownership of World Heritage sites will be bought up.

4. Culture & Community
Nowadays many nations and countries perceive culture and heritage as means to empower developing communities. This lecture discusses the conservation of indigenous or minorities cultures, and its impacts on the majority population of the same community.

5. Culture & Marketing
Culture and business are often taken as two contrasting disciplines. One of the key issues in cultural management is to develop cultural audience with both education and economic concerns. Religious sectors are a growing body of cultural venues for tourism and heritage management. This lecture discusses the debated concerns about conducting marketing or business-driven strategies in cultural and religious areas.

Section II: Case Studies
6. Cultural Management in Taiwan
Taiwan provides an excellent example to demonstrate the top-down organization of heritage sites. This lecture reviews a series of campaigns launched in Taiwan during the past twenty years, and discusses the reasons that may have contributed to engage the mass of Taiwan into different aspects of cultural industries.

7. Cultural Management in China
China represents many upcoming opportunities in cultural management. This lecture reviews some recent moves: rapid establishment of museums, growing number of commercial galleries and auction houses, rise of new Confucian schools, introduction of university degrees in cultural management, etc. The lecture discusses the consuming force underneath the cultural growth in the Mainland.

8. Cultural Management in Singapore
During the last two decades, the government of Singapore invested heavily on constructing cultural venues for both national and economic purposes. This lecture gives an overview of their establishment and invites students to reflect on the opportunities found in other areas of Asia.

9. Cultural Management in South Korea
This lecture discusses the contemporary cultural policies undertaken in South Korea. During the last decade, South Korea featured an economic miracle in Asia by rejuvenating the distressed financial market with cultural developments, which included the film industry, heritage protection, publication, and cultural tourism.

10. Cultural Management in UK
The United Kingdom was one of the earliest countries that invested heavily on promotion of cultural and arts events. This lecture gives a short history of the early developments made in the UK after the Second World War, and discusses the recent campaigns undertaken to break the boundaries between high arts and popular culture.

11. Cultural Management in USA
The United States distinguishes herself from all other countries by boosting the absence of a ministry for arts and culture, yet artists and cultural workers receive due respects for their contributions. This lecture looks at the case of the US and examines her success in cultural management.

12. Group presentation
This lecture is taken as a mock symposium for students to present their group projects and make comments on those by their peers. The presentation will be evaluated against the clarity and thoughts over the approved topics.

13. Conclusion: What is the best for Hong Kong?
This last session will summarize the topics covered throughout the course. Hong Kong is facing the challenge that many aspects of cultural developments in relation to urban planning, legislation, economy, national identity, and education are all pending. This lecture is an open discussion for students to brainstorm the possible approaches that Hong Kong could take in years to come.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Heritage and Modern Applications
courses.description:
Cultural heritage is not confined to the past but is continuously carried forward into the present and future through various modern applications. These applications address current societal concerns, needs, and the ever-changing culture both locally and globally. The relevance of cultural heritage is influenced by complex power structures, including its presentation and representation in contexts such as postcolonialism, racial dynamics, gender, intergenerational equity, disparities in access to technology, marginalization, and the tension between localism and globalization. Additionally, the modern application of cultural heritage is shaped by evolving economic structures and technological advancements. Heritage is increasingly utilized by creative industries, with its assets digitized, interpreted, and experienced through advanced technologies such as AI and VR. Ensuring the continued relevance of cultural heritage has become a critical issue.
This course aims to provide students with an understanding of cultural heritage and its diverse modern applications, along with the critical concepts that shape our perception of its relevance today. It addresses issues concerning cultural heritage and its relationship with changing urban demographics, climate change, intergenerational equity, and the application of technologies for future alternatives. Additionally, the course explores cultural heritage as an economic generator, its role in performance, sports, and games, and its adoption in personalized tours and emerging cultural industries. Through a variety of concepts and case studies, students will gain multiple perspectives on current practices and reflect on the vast potential of cultural heritage in contemporary times.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students would be able to:

* Explore key examples of cultural heritage and its diverse modern applications, along with the critical concepts that shape our perception of its relevance today.
* Understand the modern applications of cultural heritage.
* Explain cases where cultural heritage acts as an economic generator.
* Reflect on broader critical issues surrounding the modern applications of cultural heritage, including but not limited to postcolonialism, racial dynamics, and other related topics.
* Cultivate an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within existing applications and projecting future directions in cultural heritage.

courses.subject: CURE
courses.title: Special Topic in Creative Industries
courses.description:
In recent years, the rapid development of cultural and creative industries has transformed the way cultural products are created, produced and distributed. These industries, from theater and fashion to social media and game design, highlight how contemporary societies use intellectual and creative approaches to gain economic and symbolic competitiveness. Alongside technological innovations, the creative sector also plays a significant role in driving global economic transformation, offering government agencies and entrepreneurs new strategies to produce creative experiences not anticipated in the past.

This course aims to provide students with both analytical and practical skills in cultural and creative industries. Students will engage with a diverse range of topics, exploring how various sectors within these industries inform a variety of theories and practices. By covering multiple creative and entrepreneurial strategies in the ever-expanding field of cultural and creative industries, this course will equip students with the ability to reflect on the current phenomenon and create projects that have the potential to impact individuals and societies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Explain key historical and contemporary examples of creative industries, relating them to a broader local and global context
* Examine critical issues concerning how different cultural and economic models impact the creative industries
* Develop skills to critically analyze the relationship between culture, society and the economy
* Acquire personal and social competencies relating to the creative industries, and act as an active agent in producing creative projects
* Develop an attitude of innovation and creativity by challenging assumptions within the creative industries

8. Intellectual Property and Copyright Issues in a Chosen Specific Industry

9. Cultural Implications — Cultural Diversity, Privacy Issues, Equality, Labor, Environmental Issues, and Exploitation in a Chosen Specific Industry
